extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Platonic philosophy / classics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and educational program for selecting and training guardians (philosopher-rulers) as described in Plato's Republic (Books VI–VII): intellectual virtues, moral formation, curriculum (gymnastic, music, mathematics, dialectic), and the obligation to govern. Focuses on the nature of the Good, stages of cognition, and the allegory of the cave as instructional model.

rubrics_metrics.name: The perfect guardian must be a philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates: 'the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical knowledge (especially knowledge of the Good) is presented as the defining qualification for rulers: only those who have ascended to the highest knowledge are fit to govern. This is the central selection criterion that overrides mere practical success or cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess both quick intelligence and steadfastness (integrated gifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts such as quick intelligence, memory, sagacity, cleverness, high-spiritedness, magnanimity, and, on the other hand, steadfast, dependable natures seldom 'grow together' and must both be found in guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that many virtues appear in 'shreds and patches'—the ideal guardian combines lively intellect and firmness of character. Selection/testing must identify candidates who integrate these contrasting dispositions rather than only one side (e.g., cleverness without steadiness or steadiness without intellectual ardour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test in labours, dangers, and pleasures; endurance for highest studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspirants must be 'tested in those labours and dangers and pleasures' and 'exercised also in many kinds of knowledge' to see whether their soul can endure the highest knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is not merely academic: candidates must prove resilience under practical trials and across diverse studies to ensure they can bear the demands of dialectical and civic responsibility; failure under stress disqualifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the Good is the highest knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of the Good is described as 'the highest of all knowledge'—the cause of truth and science, the author of being and essence in the intellectual realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All other knowledge and possessions only become valuable through their relation to the Good. Guardians must attain, or at least reliably apprehend, the Good; without this, other virtues and knowledge are insufficient for proper governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek reality not mere appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: People may be satisfied with the 'appearance' of justice, honour, or good, but 'no one is satisfied with the appearance of good—the reality is what they seek.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must be oriented toward reality (the forms/ideas), not mere semblances. An emphasis on truthfulness, integrity, and the rejection of superficial respectability is part of the evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive understanding of the virtues in perfected form
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not behold 'the outline merely' of virtues like justice and temperance; 'nothing short of the most finished picture should satisfy us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must lead to a refined, precise grasp of the virtues—'highest accuracy'—not a crude or popular exposition. The standard demands full, nuanced understanding rather than approximate or folk definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to grasp Forms/Ideas beyond sensory appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: The many are 'seen but not known' while the ideas are 'known but not seen'; students must be able to move from opinions about images to knowledge of the forms themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive competence is measured by one's capacity to abstract from sensible particulars to intelligible essences. This entails training that increasingly privileges thought over sense-perception (geometry, dialectic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual vision: capacity to be turned toward truth (analogy of the sun)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Good is likened to the sun: it 'imparts truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower.' The soul must be able to turn toward this light and perceive truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should look for candidates who can endure and enjoy the clarity of intellectual vision—the ability to see truth as luminous rather than being content with dim opinion. This includes progressive acclimation to greater intellectual 'light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and development of higher faculties (reason over understanding/faith/perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corresponding to four divisions of cognition are four faculties—reason (highest), understanding, faith/conviction, and perception of shadows—each with differing clearness and truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education aims to elevate the soul to the faculty of reason; assessment should check where a student stands on this scale and whether they can progress toward reasoning about first principles rather than remain at opinion or hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to undergo painful intellectual conversion (allegory of the cave)
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberated prisoner suffers pains and bewilderment on being turned toward the light and must be led gradually from shadows to reflections to objects to the sun itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True education is not instantaneous or comfortable. Candidates must show the capacity to endure disorientation and difficulty during cognitive reorientation and to steadily adjust to higher truths; instructors must guide patiently and progressively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to descend and serve despite reluctance
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who attain the beatific vision 'must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den' and share in their labours and honours for the good of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crucial moral requirement: the best minds must accept duty to govern rather than remain aloof in contemplation. Evaluation includes willingness to apply knowledge in practical, often thankless, public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for rulers: prioritize the State's good over personal happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator 'did not aim at making any one class in the State happy above the rest'—the guardians should not seek a better life than others; their ruling is a duty to bind up the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers are judged by their commitment to the common good and readiness to forego private advantage; ambition for honours or wealth is an anti-pattern that undermines proper governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine philosophical knowledge with practical usefulness (e.g., war)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new kind of knowledge that draws the soul from becoming to being must, for guardian-warriors, also have 'usefulness in war'; arithmetic/number and calculation are cited as universally used by arts and sciences and therefore useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The curriculum must produce philosophers who are also practically competent: mathematical competence and other universal arts that apply to warfare and administration are required. Evaluation must include practical aptitudes, not only theoretical purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum progression: gymnastic, music, mathematics, geometry, dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier education had two parts—gymnastic (body) and music (habits)—but for rulers the sequence continues to 'number and calculation', geometry, and then dialectic which leads beyond hypotheses to first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A staged program is prescribed: bodily training and habituation (gymnastic, music) → mathematical sciences → geometry and allied arts → dialectic as the culminating study. Assessment must be stage-appropriate and confirm readiness before progressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest science: ascent to first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic moves 'out of hypotheses' to a first principle of the whole; it alone allows the soul to 'soar beyond' hypotheses and to contemplate ideas themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence in dialectical reasoning—using hypotheses only as departure points and reaching first principles—is the highest intellectual standard. Tests should evaluate capacity for dialectic rather than mere technical skill within a limited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers should be disinclined to govern; ruling only from duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The best life 'looks down upon the life of political ambition'; rulers 'ought not to be lovers of the task'—if they are, there will be rival lovers and fighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ethical criterion: the preferred rulers are those who do not crave office. Assessment includes motive examination: those eager to rule for glory or gain are unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early moral formation: removal of sensual impediments and habit-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: If clever but sensual natures had been 'severed from those sensual pleasures' in youth and turned away from 'eating and drinking' pleasures that 'drag them down', their faculties would have seen truth as keenly as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and habit formation in youth is essential—education must curb sensual indulgence and cultivate right orientations. Selection and training must include moral regulation and formative practices to eliminate impediments to intellectual vision.
